cim: Amatőr csillagászok 49 jelölt exobolygót találtak az OpenAI eszközeivel
lead: Két amatőr kutató az OpenAI Astra és Codex eszközeivel 19 millió csillag adatát elemezte, és több tucat lehetséges új bolygót azonosított.
osszefoglalo:
Két amatőr kutató az OpenAI fejlett mesterséges intelligencia modelljeit hívta segítségül a **NASA adatbázisainak** elemzéséhez. Ethan Byrd az **Astra** segítségével 19 millió csillag megfigyelési adatait dolgozta fel, és 49 lehetséges exobolygó-jelöltet azonosított. Kevin Bond, az OpenAI mérnöke a [Codex](https://openai.com/codex) segítségével írt keresőprogramot, amellyel a Kepler űrtávcső 100 000 csillagának adataiban talált több mint 200 gyanús jelet.

A kutatók a tranzitmetódust alkalmazták, amely a csillagok fényerejének időszakos csökkenését méri, amikor egy bolygó áthalad előttük. A talált jelek között szerepel a KIC 5689121 jelű csillag is, amelynél egy 13,8 naponta ismétlődő elhalványodást észleltek: ez egy, a **Földnél 2,4-szer nagyobb** bolygóra utalhat. A SETI Intézet szakértői már függetlenül is megerősítették a jelek jelenlétét.

Az eredmények még nem jelentik új bolygók hivatalos felfedezését, a jelöltek most **professzionális csillagászokhoz** kerültek további mérésekre és ellenőrzésre. A fényességcsökkenést ugyanis kettőscsillagok vagy műszeres zajok is okozhatják, így a végső igazoláshoz további spektroszkópiai vizsgálatokra lesz szükség.
miert_szamit: A hír jól mutatja, hogy az AI-kódgeneráló és elemző eszközökkel **bárki számára elérhetővé válik a komplex tudományos adatbányászat**, ami új lehetőségeket nyit a közösségi kutatásokban.

cim_eredeti: Amateur astronomers use OpenAI to spot 49 hidden planet candidates
szoveg_eredeti:
Two amateur astronomers used OpenAI's Astra and Codex to search public telescope data for potential exoplanets.

Ethan Byrd used Astra to analyze observations covering approximately 19 million stars, identifying 49 potential planet candidates.

OpenAI engineer Kevin Bond used Codex to examine data from around 100,000 stars observed by NASA's Kepler Space Telescope.

Two amateur astronomers have identified dozens of potential exoplanets using OpenAI’s Astra and Codex to analyze data from NASA telescope missions. Their searches examined observations covering approximately 19 million stars and produced several candidates awaiting independent verification.

One search identified 49 potential planets in its initial results. Another flagged more than 200 signals in Kepler observations, including two candidates that attracted independent attention from an astronomer at the SETI Institute.

Neither researcher has confirmed a new exoplanet. However, their findings have reached professional astronomers for further investigation.Two independent searches

Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, used Codex to develop a search program analyzing data from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope. His investigation covered approximately 100,000 stars observed during the mission’s 2009–2018 operational period.

Two amateur astronomers, Kevin Bond (@canvrno) and Ethan Byrd (@itsjustemail), independently found signals that could point to planets around distant stars. They knew you didn't need your own telescope for this kind of hunt.Kevin used Codex and Ethan used Astra to search public… pic.twitter.com/Wpw7xPHLmf

The program identified more than 200 signals, including 10 associated with previously confirmed planets. Two additional candidates stood out during subsequent analysis.

One involves KIC 5689121, a relatively cool star in the constellation Lyra. The search detected a recurring dip in its brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet causes the signal, it could measure approximately 2.4 times Earth’s diameter.

Bond shared his findings with the SETI Institute for independent assessment. Associate director Vishal Gajjar conducted a separate search and identified two matching signals in the Kepler dataset.

Gajjar said Bond’s work had surfaced promising candidates that traditional searches might have missed. Follow-up observations will help researchers determine whether the signals indicate actual planets.

Ethan Byrd, founder of email infrastructure startup Primitive, conducted a separate investigation using OpenAI’s Astra. His searches covered observations of approximately 19 million stars.

Byrd used Astra to examine published astronomical methods and develop two search programs. One targeted exoplanet candidates broadly, while the other focused on stars with potentially habitable zones.

His initial analysis identified 49 candidates. Byrd submitted one of his strongest findings to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. Two additional candidates are awaiting submission.

Both investigations relied on the transit method, which detects planets through changes in their host stars’ brightness. A planet passing between its star and Earth blocks a small amount of starlight.

That crossing creates a dip in measurements known as a light curve. Repeated dips at regular intervals can indicate an orbiting planet.

Similar signals can also originate from other astronomical objects or instrumental disturbances. Two stars passing in front of each other can produce comparable brightness changes. Temperature fluctuations inside a telescope can also affect its measurements.

Astronomers therefore need additional observations before confirming a candidate. They can monitor subsequent transits or measure subtle movements in a star caused by an orbiting planet’s gravity. The latter technique, known as radial velocity, detects changes in a star’s light spectrum as it moves toward or away from Earth.
